name: Moánus
confidence_why: The only first-hand remark on accent, Meier 1906, is an aside that Schnee 1901's doubled consonants merely follow the stressed syllable, and the one modern description with a stress section, Bowern 2011, was not available to read, so no placement or type of word stress can be defended for Titan.
catalog_citation: Meier, P. Josef. 1906. Berichtigungen zu Dr. Schnee's Mitteilungen über die Sprache der Moánus (Admiralitäts-Inseln). Anthropos 1: 210-228, 472-482.
catalog_locator: Anthropos 1 (1906): 216, general remark 9 (remarks 1-13 precede section 'A. Die Moánus-Sprache'); copy consulted, p. 7
catalog_quote: 9. Hin und wieder bringt Dr. Schnee in seinem Material Konsonanten-Verdoppelungen. Dieselben können füglich umgangen werden. Der Laut s, der zudem etwas wie h-s klingt, ist immer scharf. Ebenso wird r immer scharf gesprochen. In diesen beiden Fällen wird also die Notwendigkeit, eine Verdoppelung zu schreiben, durch diesen Hinweis bereits gehoben. Wo sich sonst noch Verdoppelungen bei Dr. Schnee finden, sind dieselben durch den Akzent überflüssig gemacht, der regelmäßig auf der Verdoppelung der vorhergehenden Silbe ruht.

new_statements.translation: 9. Now and then Dr. Schnee gives consonant doublings in his material. These can reasonably be dispensed with. The sound s, which moreover sounds something like h-s, is always sharp. Likewise r is always pronounced sharp. In these two cases the need to write a doubling is thus already removed by this note. Where doublings are otherwise still found in Dr. Schnee, they are made superfluous by the accent, which regularly rests on the syllable preceding the doubling (literally: 'on the doubling of the preceding syllable').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Not a placement rule. Meier only says that Schnee's written geminates mark nothing but the accent on the syllable before them, and that he instead marks the accent with an acute on every word. His accent-marked forms (lépan, léwan, Móuk, Mínis, Moánus, Matánkor, tjórer vs. suffixed matajé) would allow a rule to be inferred, but no source I could open states one; Bowern 2011 §2.5 'Lexical Stress' (pp. 13-24 range) is the description of record and is paywalled.
new_statements.domain_note: Meier's remark concerns single words in a corrected wordlist (Moánus dialect of Po Minis, Fedarb Islands/Siwisa); the accent marks appear on citation forms and in running text of the 1907-1909 tales.
new_statements.identity_note: Meier's 1906 data are the Moánus (= Titan) speech of his informant Po Minis, whose mother's home was Siwisa (Sivisa) in the Fedarb Islands; Meier explicitly separates this from the Móuk-dialect of Schnee's informant Po Kitjong and from Matánkor (a different language) — Bowern's title 'Sivisa Titan' names the same Sivisa dialect. Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect languoids under tita1241; alternate names Moanus, Manus, M'bunai, Tito.

tone_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Titan is not a tonal language. Primary stress is manifested as a higher pitch and tends to fall on the penultimate syllable, except in three-syllable words where it falls on the first syllable. No examples of contrastive stress have been found.

sources.note: No phonology section; 13 numbered orthographic/phonetic remarks (pp. 214-217). Point 9 (p. 216) is the only accent statement: Schnee's written consonant doublings are made superfluous by 'the accent, which regularly rests on the [syllable preceding the] doubling'. Every Moánus word in the article carries an acute accent mark (lépan/léwan 'chief', matajé, Móuk, Mínis, Matánkor, Moánus, Usíai, tjórer), i.e. an accent-marked corpus, but no general placement rule is stated. Part 2 (pp. 472-482) has no accent remark.

tone.quote: Meier (1906:472-82) gives a few example sentences and a very short text on which stress is notated. It is reproduced here as 1.6 in Section II on page 218. Stress is also marked on the numerals and pronouns in the grammatical sketch. From this very small sample, stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word, or, in the case of compounds, on the head of the compound. There is also a reduplicated word, susunai, on which stress appears to be variable [...]. Lusk (nd) marks stress fairly consistently on the penult. The same stress pattern is found in Loniu (Hamel 1994:23-25), although Kele (Ross 2002:125) appears to have lexically specific stress which varies between the final syllable and the penult.
